title: Standard Normal Distribution

blocks.title: Properties of a Normal Distribution
teacherCues: Ask: 'What shape comes to mind when you hear bell curve?'
Draw two normal curves with different means and standard deviations. Ask: 'Which has the greater mean? Which is more spread out?'

discoveryHook.scenario: From human blood pressure to the lifetimes of televisions, many real-world measurements follow a bell-shaped pattern. This pattern, called a normal distribution, is the most important continuous probability distribution in statistics—it helps us model everything from test scores to housing costs!

explanation: A [[kw:normal distribution]] is a continuous probability distribution for a random variable $x$. Its graph is called a normal curve.
The mean, median, and mode are all equal.
The normal curve is bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean.
The total area under the curve is 1.
The curve approaches but never touches the x-axis as it extends away from the mean.
Between $\mu - \sigma$ and $\mu + \sigma$, the graph curves downward. The points where curvature changes are [[kw:inflection points]].

rows.1: Bell-shaped and symmetric about the mean

examples.title: A – Compare Two Normal Curves
examples.prompt: Two normal curves A and B have lines of symmetry at $x=15$ and $x=12$. Which has the greater mean? If B is more spread out, which has the greater standard deviation?
steps: The mean is the line of symmetry. Curve A has line at $x=15$, curve B at $x=12$.
So curve A has the greater mean.
Greater spread means greater standard deviation. So curve B has the greater standard deviation.

examples.title: B – Inflection Points
examples.prompt: Explain what inflection points are on a normal curve and where they occur.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why do the inflection points help you estimate the standard deviation?
steps: Inflection points are where the curve changes from curving downward to curving upward.
They occur at one standard deviation from the mean: $\mu - \sigma$ and $\mu + \sigma$.
The distance from the mean to an inflection point is the standard deviation.

examples.title: C – Estimate Mean and Standard Deviation
examples.prompt: A normal curve is symmetric at $x=675$. Inflection points appear near $x=640$ and $x=710$. Estimate the mean and standard deviation.
steps: Mean $\mu$ is the line of symmetry: 675.
Distance from mean to inflection point: $710 - 675 = 35$.

confusionCorner.title: Mean vs. Standard Deviation
confusionCorner.body: The mean tells you the center; the standard deviation tells you the spread. Two curves can have the same mean but different standard deviations, or the same spread but different centers.

questions.prompt: The total area under a normal curve is ___.
In a normal distribution, are the mean, median, and mode equal? (yes/no)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Yes, they are all equal in a normal distribution.

questions.prompt: If curve A is more spread out than curve B, which has the greater standard deviation?
hints: Spread is measured by standard deviation.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Curve A has the greater standard deviation.

blocks.title: The Standard Normal Distribution
teacherCues: Define standard normal: mean 0, standard deviation 1.
Write z-score formula on board and demonstrate with a sample x-value.

discoveryHook.scenario: With infinitely many possible normal distributions, how can we compare them? The standard normal distribution—mean 0, standard deviation 1—provides a common yardstick. By converting any x-value to a z-score, we can use one table to find probabilities for any normal distribution!

explanation: The [[kw:standard normal distribution]] is a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
The horizontal scale of the standard normal curve is labeled with [[kw:z-scores]].
A z-score tells how many standard deviations a value is from the mean: $$ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} $$
Transform any normally distributed x-value to a z-score, and the standard normal curve can be used to find probabilities.
The standard normal curve has total area 1 centered at 0.

formulaCard.title: Z-Score
notes: Round z to the nearest hundredth.

examples.title: A – Convert to Z-Score
examples.prompt: For a normal distribution with $\mu = 100$ and $\sigma = 15$, find the z-score for $x = 118$.

examples.title: B – Interpret a Negative Z-Score
examples.prompt: For the same distribution, explain the meaning of a z-score of -2.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does a negative z-score mean the x-value is below the mean?
steps: A negative z-score means $x$ is less than the mean.

examples.title: C – Find Z-Score
examples.prompt: Scores on a test have $\mu = 500$ and $\sigma = 100$. Find the z-score for a score of 650.

confusionCorner.title: Raw Score vs. Z-Score
confusionCorner.body: A raw score $x$ is in the original units. A z-score tells how many standard deviations $x$ is from the mean. The standard normal distribution uses z-scores, not raw scores.

questions.prompt: The standard normal distribution has a mean of ___ and a standard deviation of 1.
If $\mu = 50$, $\sigma = 5$, and $x = 60$, what is the z-score?
If a z-score is negative, is the x-value above or below the mean?
hints: Negative means less than the mean.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: A negative z-score means below the mean.

blocks.title: Using the Standard Normal Table
teacherCues: Show how to find area for z = 1.15 using table.
Demonstrate area to left, right, and between z-scores with sketches.

discoveryHook.scenario: The standard normal table lists cumulative areas to the left of any z-score from -3.49 to 3.49. With this table, you can find the area under the curve in any region—left, right, or between—turning z-scores into probabilities!

explanation: The standard normal table gives the cumulative area to the left of a z-score.
To find area to the left of z: look up z directly in the table.
To find area to the right of z: find area to left, then subtract from 1.
To find area between two z-scores: find area to left of each, then subtract smaller from larger.
When z is not in the table, use the closest entry or average if midway.

visuals.title: Finding Areas Under Standard Normal Curve

rows.1: Look up z in table directly

formulaCard.title: Area Rules
formulaCard.formula: $$ P(z < a) = \text{table value} $$ $$ P(z > a) = 1 - P(z < a) $$ $$ P(a < z < b) = P(z < b) - P(z < a) $$
notes: Table gives area to the left.

examples.title: A – Area to the Left
examples.prompt: Find the cumulative area for z = 1.15.
steps: In the standard normal table, find row 1.1 and column 0.05.
So the area to the left of z = 1.15 is 0.8749.

examples.title: B – Area to the Right
examples.prompt: Find the area to the right of z = 1.06.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why do you subtract the table value from 1?
steps: Table gives area to left of z = 1.06 as 0.8554.

examples.title: C – Area Between Two Z-Scores
examples.prompt: Find the area between z = -1.5 and z = 1.25.
steps: Area to left of z = 1.25 is 0.8944.
Area to left of z = -1.5 is 0.0668.

confusionCorner.title: Left vs. Right
confusionCorner.body: The table always gives area to the left. For area to the right, always subtract from 1. A common mistake is to forget the subtraction.

questions.prompt: The standard normal table gives the cumulative area to the ___ of a z-score.
hints: It is the direction the area is accumulated from -∞.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The table gives area to the left.

questions.prompt: If the area to the left of z = 1.5 is 0.9332, what is the area to the right?
What is the area to the left of z = 0?
hints: It is the center of the distribution.
Half the area is on each side.

blocks.title: Finding Areas and Probabilities
teacherCues: Show how area under normal curve equals probability.
Demonstrate unusual events: z > 2 or z < -2 are unusual; z > 3 or z < -3 very unusual.

discoveryHook.scenario: The area under the normal curve is probability. If you know the z-score, you know the probability of observing that value or less. Values more than two standard deviations from the mean are unusual—more than three are very unusual!

explanation: The area under the standard normal curve to the left of a z-score gives $P(z < \text{that z-score})$.
Use the table to find probabilities for any region.
A z-score greater than 2 or less than -2 indicates an [[imp:unusual]] value.
A z-score greater than 3 or less than -3 indicates a [[imp:very unusual]] value.
Technology can also compute these probabilities directly.

formulaCard.title: Probability from Area
formulaCard.formula: $$ P(z < a) = \text{area to left of } a $$

examples.title: A – Probability Less Than
steps: From the standard normal table, area to left of z = -0.99 is 0.1611.

examples.title: B – Probability Greater Than
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why is this equal to 1 minus the table value for 1.23?

examples.title: C – Unusual Event
steps: Not greater than 3, so not very unusual.

confusionCorner.title: Area = Probability
confusionCorner.body: For continuous distributions, probability is area under the curve. $P(z < a)$ is exactly the area to the left of $a$. There is no difference between 'less than' and 'less than or equal to' for continuous variables.

questions.prompt: In a continuous probability distribution, probability is represented by ___ under the curve.
hints: It is found using the table.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Probability is area under the curve.

questions.prompt: Is a z-score of -2.7 unusual or very unusual?
hints: It is more than 2 but less than 3 in magnitude.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: -2.7 is unusual, but not very unusual because it is not less than -3.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Solving Normal Distribution Problems
teacherCues: Display Understand → Solve → Conclude. Walk through a z-score and probability problem.
Emphasize: Understand identifies mean, standard deviation, and region. Solve converts to z and finds area. Conclude interprets probability.

discoveryHook.scenario: With the standard normal table, you can find the probability of nearly any normally distributed event. The blueprint helps you organize: Understand the problem, Solve using z-scores and the table, and Conclude with the probability and whether it is unusual.

explanation: [[imp:Understand]] – Read the problem. Identify the mean $\mu$, standard deviation $\sigma$, the raw score $x$, and the region (left, right, between).
[[imp:Solve]] – Convert $x$ to z-score: $z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$. Use the standard normal table or technology to find the area.
[[imp:Conclude]] – State the probability. Determine if the event is unusual (|z| > 2). Interpret in context.

rows.1: Compute z-score; use table for area.

examples.title: A – Full Blueprint: Probability
examples.prompt: Use blueprint: Normal distribution with $\mu = 100$, $\sigma = 15$. Find probability x is less than 118.

examples.title: B – Full Blueprint: Right Tail
examples.prompt: Use blueprint: Test scores with $\mu = 500$, $\sigma = 100$. Find probability score is greater than 650.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: After finding the z-score, why do you subtract from 1?
steps: Conclude: Probability is 0.0668. Not unusual since z = 1.5 < 2.

examples.title: C – Decide and Compute
examples.prompt: Use blueprint: Heights have $\mu = 65$ inches, $\sigma = 3$ inches. Find probability height is less than 59 inches.

confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget to Convert
confusionCorner.body: Never use raw x-values directly in the standard normal table. Always convert to z-scores first. The table is built for z-scores, not raw scores.

questions.prompt: What is the first thing you identify in the Understand phase?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Identify the mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

questions.prompt: In the Solve phase, convert the raw score $x$ to a ___ using the formula $z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

presenterNotes: Start with the intuition of the bell curve. Draw several curves to show how mean and standard deviation affect shape.
The standard normal table is central. Practice reading it with students for various z-scores.
Emphasize the difference between area to the left, right, and between z-scores. Use sketches to reinforce.
Connect z-scores back to Empirical Rule: z = ±1, ±2, ±3 correspond to 68%, 95%, 99.7%.
The blueprint helps students remember to convert to z-scores before using the table.
